title: Alcohol: Why Islam's Position Differs from Most Christian Denominations
summary: Comparing the Islamic prohibition on alcohol with the range of Christian positions, from communion wine to full abstinence traditions.

body.text: A practical difference reverts navigate immediately

Opening this section on ethics and daily life: alcohol is often one of the first, most immediately practical adjustments a revert makes, especially around family gatherings and holidays — worth understanding clearly, including how it compares to the actual range of Christian positions rather than an assumed single Christian view.
The Islamic position: a clear, complete prohibition
Islamic teaching prohibits alcohol consumption entirely — not just drunkenness, but any amount of intoxicating drink — a position all major Sunni schools of law agree on without significant dispute.

body.translation: O you who have believed, indeed, intoxicants, gambling, [sacrificing on] stone altars, and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may be successful.

body.text: The actual range of Christian positions

There isn't one single Christian position on alcohol — Catholic, Orthodox, and many mainline Protestant traditions permit moderate alcohol use and use actual wine in communion, drawing on Jesus' own recorded wine-drinking and the wedding at Cana; other traditions, particularly some Baptist, Methodist (historically), and evangelical communities, teach full abstinence or at least strong caution, some using grape juice for communion specifically to avoid alcohol. Reverts from an already-abstaining Christian background may find this specific Islamic requirement a smaller practical adjustment than reverts coming from a tradition that used alcohol, including sacramentally.
Why Islam draws the line at prohibition rather than moderation

Islamic reasoning generally centers on alcohol's capacity to impair judgment and disrupt the clear-mindedness required for prayer and righteous living, alongside its well-documented social harms — leading to prohibition rather than a moderation-based approach some Christian traditions take. This reflects a broader pattern in Islamic ethics of preferring clear, decisive lines over case-by-case moderation for things assessed as carrying significant potential harm.

body.question: What about communion wine — is that also off-limits, or can it be seen as a special exception?
body.answer: Since a revert no longer participates in Christian communion as a matter of changed belief (covered earlier in this collection), this specific tension doesn't typically arise in practice — but the Islamic prohibition itself makes no religious-context exception for sacramental use.

body.question: How do I handle family gatherings where alcohol is served?
body.answer: Most converts find that simply declining a drink while participating fully in everything else at the gathering is well received, especially once family understands it as a firm religious commitment rather than a judgment on their own choices; bringing your own non-alcoholic drink to share can also help normalise the adjustment.
